Steinhaus' Problem

FractionsLogicCounting
Game: Put numbered tiles on a line so that the first two are in different halves, the first three in different thirds, and so on. How many can you place?
How to play: Drag the next tile from the box onto the line; drag placed tiles to move them. The line shows the pieces for the tiles placed so far.
Look for the math

Hugo Steinhaus, in One Hundred Problems in Elementary Mathematics, asked for numbers x₁, x₂, … in [0, 1] such that for every k the first k of them lie in different k-ths of the interval. He gave two solutions with ten numbers and asked whether ten could be beaten.

Only the pieces matter

Whether a list works depends only on which piece each number falls in, for each k: x is in the ⌊kx⌋-th k-th. So each new number narrows down the places every earlier number may still go, and a computer can try every possibility exactly, with all the fractions written over the common denominator lcm(1, …, 18).

Seventeen is the limit

M. Warmus proved that 17 numbers are possible and 18 are not. Berlekamp and Graham later proved a general theorem on the irregularity of distribution that implies it, and Richard Guy published the 17 in the Examples list. The logic test ran that exact search: it found a list for every length up to 17 and proved, in a complete search, that no list of 18 exists. The page's five examples all pass the applet's check.

Why it gets hard

Spreading numbers evenly is easy for one k at a time: put them in the middles of the pieces. The difficulty is that the same first numbers must be well spread for every k at once. Each new number has to fill the one piece left empty, and that keeps pushing the early numbers into ever narrower slots, as in the pigeonhole principle.

Start Steinhaus's second ten (.06, .55, .77, …) and try to add an eleventh number yourself before looking at the fourteen.
